1) iPhone Duo is Apple's big foldable swing

Let's start with the product everyone is talking about. iPhone Duo opens to a 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR display. Apple says that gives you 50% more screen area than iPhone 18 Pro Max. The 5.4-inch outer display offers 90% of the screen area of iPhone 18 Pro.

Apple also tackled one of the biggest complaints about foldables: the crease. The company developed a custom nano-texture finish that reduces glare and reflections. Apple says the finish also minimizes the visibility of the crease while giving the display a matte feel.

There are some other unexpected choices. Instead of Face ID, iPhone Duo uses Touch ID built into the side button. You can enroll multiple fingers, so unlocking works in different positions. Apple Pencil with USB-C support will arrive later this year. The phone uses Grade 5 titanium. Apple also says it carries an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance.

The folding design also creates some camera tricks you can't get on a regular iPhone. Dual Capture can show your front and rear camera feeds at the same time during FaceTime, while Duo FaceTime lets someone beside you join the call using the outer display. You can also use that outer screen to frame higher-quality selfies with the rear cameras.

Apple added a few other clever touches. Duo Preview lets the person you're photographing see the shot before you take it, while Kid Cue uses animations to get a child's attention. Smart Take can even watch the scene and automatically snap a photo when everyone is ready. Then comes the part that may give you sticker shock: the price. iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage. Apple will offer configurations up to 2TB. Preorders begin Oct. 16, with availability starting Oct. 23.
2) Apple redesigned iOS around the fold

The hardware grabs your eye, but the software could decide whether Duo succeeds. Apple changed iOS 27 so content moves between the outside and inside displays. Open the phone and apps can expand onto the larger screen.
You can also put two apps side by side. Mail can show your inbox alongside a message. The Home Screen can display two pages at once. The system also responds when you fold or rotate the phone.

That caught my attention because a folding screen needs to earn its extra cost. If I open a phone this large, I want more than a bigger version of the same app. Apple is also giving developers tools to take advantage of the design. During the event, Apple showed Zoom using the expanded screen for video calls and Netflix adapting its experience to the two displays.

The cameras use the second screen too. Duo Preview lets the person you're photographing see themselves on the outer display. Meanwhile, Smart Take can follow a scene and automatically snap the photo when everyone looks ready. Those are the features that could make the folding design useful after the initial wow factor wears off.
Apple CEO John Ternus displays the iPhone Duo on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, on the Apple campus in Cupertino, Calif. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)
3) iPhone 18 Pro gets much more serious about photography

If a foldable phone doesn't interest you, Apple gave the regular Pro lineup a substantial camera upgrade. The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max use a 48MP Fusion Main camera with a variable aperture.

The camera can automatically adjust the aperture depending on lighting and depth of field. Apple also gives photographers manual control through four aperture settings: ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8 and ƒ/4.0.
In darker environments, opening the aperture lets in more light. A narrower aperture can keep more of a scene in focus. However, another camera feature may prove even more important.

Apple Reference Image securely signs photo data at the pixel level when the picture is captured. Apple says that can help verify exactly what the camera sensor saw. Think about where we're headed with AI-generated images.

Being able to verify that an image began as an actual camera capture could become valuable for journalists, investigators or anyone documenting something important. That feature may get less attention than the new camera hardware. I wouldn't overlook it.
iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299. Preorders begin Sept. 12, with both phones available starting Sept. 18.
APPLE RAISES PRICES AS AI CHIP COSTS SURGE
4) Battery life may be the iPhone 18 Pro upgrade you feel most

Apple can show us faster chips every year. Most of us notice battery life much faster. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max can deliver up to 45 hours of video playback, the longest battery life the company has offered in an iPhone. It also rates the Pro Max for up to 30 hours of general use per charge.
Charging gets faster too. Apple says iPhone 18 Pro can reach 50% charge in around 15 minutes with a compatible adapter. Underneath it all sits the A20 Pro chip.

Apple built A20 Pro using 2-nanometer technology. The chip includes a second Neural Engine, bringing the total to 32 Neural Engine cores. Apple says that doubles compute power for advanced on-device models. The new Pro models also use a redesigned vapor chamber to manage heat. Faster performance sounds good. More time away from a charger is something you'll notice every day.
5) Siri AI is moving from keynote promise to everyday use

Siri AI had a big role in Apple's Sept. 9 iPhone 18 Pro unveiling. Apple showed how its rebuilt assistant can use your personal context, understand what you're looking at and take action across the apps you already use.

During the event, Apple showed someone asking what her mother wanted to cook during an upcoming visit. Siri searched Mail and Messages to find the answer. Apple also demonstrated Siri working through the Camera app. Point your iPhone at something and Siri can answer questions about what you're seeing or take action based on what's around you.

There's also a new Siri app on the Home Screen. You can use it to start a conversation or return to an earlier one, with conversations syncing privately through iCloud. Siri AI begins rolling out in beta in English on Sept. 14 with iOS 27. Apple says support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish will follow in October.
Apple CEO John Ternus speaks during an announcement of new products on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in Cupertino, Calif. (AP Photo/Jeff Chiu)
6) Siri Recap may start a big privacy conversation

This one made me pay attention. Apple announced Siri Recap for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. It uses ambient listening to turn conversations into high-level notes. Apple says each recap can include a title, summary and key points that appear in the Siri app. You control where and when Siri Recap takes notes. For example, you could allow it at work but disable it at night.

Then there is Live Rewind. Double-click the Digital Crown and Apple Watch can transcribe what was said during the previous 15 seconds. You can then review what you missed. That's useful if you missed something someone said in a noisy restaurant. Naturally, ambient listening raises privacy questions.

Apple says these Audio Intelligence features do not create or store audio recordings. The company says raw audio used for processing remains inaccessible, even to Apple. Apple also says Audio Intelligence does not identify or attribute speakers. Live Rewind transcripts and Siri Recaps use end-to-end encryption when syncing through iCloud.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind require Siri AI. Apple says both will arrive in beta later this year, starting in English. I like the idea of getting help remembering an important conversation. However, I would want to know exactly when the feature is active every time I use it.
7) Apple Watch gets smarter about your health

Apple Watch is becoming more aggressive about turning health data into something you can understand. Series 12 and Ultra 4 use Apple's new Health Sensing System. According to Apple, Apple Watch Series 12 can now measure heart rate every five seconds throughout the day. Apple also says heart rate variability is measured up to 24 times more often than before. Apple says its head-to-head testing found the system delivered the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable.

For everyday users, Readiness may be the more relatable feature. Each morning, Apple Watch analyzes your recent activity, sleep and vital signs. It then gives you a score designed to help you decide whether to push harder or recover. The score can also change during the day.

Meanwhile, Apple Watch Ultra 4 gets up to 50 hours of normal use. Max Extended Workout mode can reach 45 hours. Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at $799. Both are available to preorder now and will be available starting Sept. 18.

Apple also showed how the iPhone and Apple Watch can work together to assess how your body is moving. With Movement Evaluations in the redesigned Health app, you can position your iPhone so the camera can see you, then follow guided exercises while vision-based AI analyzes your movements.

Apple says the assessments can look at flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics and VO2 max. They can also help you track your progress while recovering from an injury. Apple says the processing happens on your device, and no video is recorded, stored or shared.
SAMSUNG GALAXY Z FOLD8 LINEUP ADDS THREE CHOICES

Apple CEO John Ternus speaks during the keynote address at Apple’s "Surprise and Shine" event at the company's corporate headquarters, Apple Park, on September 9, 2026, in Cupertino, California. The event featured Apple product announcements and was Apple CEO John Ternus’s first keynote address in his new role. (Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images)
8) AirPods 5 could be one of the event's better values

The final surprise may appeal to people who have no interest in spending $1,999 on a foldable phone. Apple announced AirPods 5 with Active Noise Cancellation for $129. Apple says the new earbuds provide stronger Active Noise Cancellation than the previous generation. They keep an open-ear design for people who prefer not to use silicone ear tips. The standard $129 model gets up to four hours of listening with ANC enabled. The charging case brings the total to up to 20 hours.

A $149 version adds volume swipe on the stem and a wireless charging case. It gets up to five hours per charge with ANC and up to 22 hours with the case and ANC enabled. Both versions are available starting Sept. 18, with preorders open now.
AirPods 5 also support Live Translation and Siri AI. During the event, Apple showed AirPods translating Spanish into English while the wearer continued a face-to-face conversation.
Compared with iPhone Duo, AirPods 5 may seem like a smaller announcement. Still, the $129 model could end up being one of the products far more people actually buy.
Kurt's key takeaways

Apple gave us plenty to talk about, but iPhone Duo is the one people are going to want to pick up and play with. I certainly do. At $1,999, it carries a premium price, but Apple is clearly betting that the larger screen and new foldable experiences will be enough to tempt early adopters. What interests me more is how much smarter these devices are becoming. Siri AI finally looks like it could understand enough about your day to be genuinely helpful. Siri Recap sounds incredibly convenient too, but a watch that can summarize conversations around you deserves some healthy scrutiny about when it's listening and how clearly you know it's active. Then there are improvements you don't need a demo to appreciate. Give me longer iPhone battery life any day. And Apple Reference Image could become far more important than it sounds today if we reach a point where you can no longer trust your eyes to tell whether a photo is real.

title: What your HOA may be putting online about you
summary: Homeowners' association meeting minutes and membership lists can expose names, addresses and emails that scammers use to craft convincing phishing scams.
story: California homeowners Amy and Chris Cooke discuss their homeowners' association allegedly threatening them with fines over displaying a U.S. flag on ‘Fox News @ Night.’
A scammer doesn't need to hack your homeowners' association. They may only need to look at information your community already makes available.

Meeting minutes, membership records and other association documents can contain details about the people who live in a community. Depending on the HOA and state law, some records may be available to association members while others could appear on an association website or another online system.

You probably didn't put the information there yourself. You may have no idea how much someone can learn about you. Yet a name tied to an address or community can give a scammer useful details for making a call or message sound legitimate.
What your HOA puts online could reveal more about you than you realize. Here's what to look for and what you can do about it.
THE ONE THING SCAMMERS CHECK BEFORE TARGETING YOU ONLINE
Homeowners' associations may publish records that expose names, addresses and contact details scammers can use to make fraud attempts more convincing. (Jordan Vonderhaar/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
How HOA records can expose your personal information
HOA records can contain details about homeowners, association business and community disputes. What members can access and what an association can publish depends heavily on state law.

HOA meeting minutes and other association records can reveal more than homeowners expect. How much information appears depends on the association and state law. Some states give HOA members broad rights to inspect association records. Sensitive disciplinary, collection and payment issues can receive additional privacy protections.

California provides a useful example. State law treats board meeting minutes as association records available for member inspection but excludes minutes and other information from executive sessions. Those closed sessions can cover matters such as member discipline, certain payment issues and other sensitive association business.

California law also allows an association to withhold or redact information when releasing it could reasonably lead to identity theft or fraud or compromise a member's privacy. The privacy concern grows when an association includes unnecessary personal details in records or makes information available more broadly than required.

HOA membership lists can contain information that scammers and data brokers would find useful. In California, state law defines the membership list as including a homeowner's name, property address, mailing address and email address as collected by the association. Members can request access to association records under state law.

Homeowners also have an important privacy option. California law allows members to opt out of sharing their name, property address, mailing address and email address through the membership list by notifying the association in writing. The law also restricts association records from being sold, used for commercial purposes or used for purposes unrelated to a member's interests as a member.

Rules differ from state to state, so check the laws where you live and ask your HOA exactly what information it collects, who can access it and whether you can opt out. The concern extends beyond the HOA itself. Once personal information appears publicly online, it can be indexed or copied and combined with information already collected from public records and other sources. Data brokers and people-search sites build profiles using many of those sources.
FIVE DATA BROKER OPT-OUT MYTHS THAT LEAVE RETIREES EXPOSED
Experts warn homeowners to review what their HOA publishes online and understand available privacy protections. (PC Photography / Getty Images)
How HOA information can make scams more convincing

Personal information gives scammers context they can use to make a fraudulent message feel legitimate. The Justice Department has already prosecuted companies that supplied consumer information to fraud operations.

Epsilon Data Management, one of the largest marketing companies in the country, agreed to pay $150 million after federal prosecutors said it sold consumer data to operators running fraudulent mass-mailing schemes involving fake sweepstakes and astrology solicitations. The government said many victims were elderly and vulnerable. A related company, Macromark, pleaded guilty after lists it provided to fraudulent clients resulted in at least $9.5 million in victim losses.

Those cases involved marketing databases rather than HOA records. Still, they demonstrate why personal details can become valuable to criminals. Names and addresses helped fraudsters identify and target potential victims.

HOA information can give scammers another source of context. A scammer who learns your name, street address and community can weave those details into a phone call, text or email. A message claiming to involve an assessment or another issue connected to your property can sound far more believable when the person contacting you already knows where you live.

Older adults remain especially attractive targets for financial scammers. The FBI says criminals may target older Americans because many have accumulated significant savings. Older victims can also be more likely to engage with unsolicited phone calls, texts or emails.

In 2025, Americans over 60 reported more than $7.7 billion in internet-enabled fraud losses. The FBI received more than 201,000 complaints from people in that age group, which reported the highest total losses of any age group.

Those numbers don't mean everyone living in a retirement or 55+ community will encounter fraud. They do show why reducing unnecessary personal information online deserves attention. The fewer details scammers can easily connect to you, the harder you make their job.
How to reduce your HOA privacy exposure
You may have more control over your HOA information than you realize, but your options depend on where you live and how your association handles its records.

Start by seeing what someone outside your community can find. Search your HOA's name along with terms such as "minutes," "directory," "membership list" or your own name. Check whether documents appear directly in search results without requiring a resident login. Pay particular attention to documents that connect your name with your address or other personal information.

Contact your board or management company and ask which records anyone on the internet can access. Find out which documents require a resident login and whether search engines can index anything posted on the association's website. If a document contains personal information that has no reason to appear publicly, ask whether the association can remove it, redact the information or restrict access.

Privacy rights vary by state, so find out what options apply where you live. California homeowners, for example, can opt out of sharing certain information through the HOA membership list. Other states may have different rules covering association directories and member records. Ask your HOA or management company how its opt-out process works and whether you can limit the contact information available to other members.
WHY CAREFUL PEOPLE STILL END UP ON DATA BROKER SITES
Homeowners can reduce privacy risks by reviewing HOA policies, opting out where allowed and removing data from broker sites. (David Ryder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Even if your HOA removes information from a public page, your name, address and other details may already appear elsewhere online. People-search sites and data brokers gather personal information from public records, websites and other sources, then combine those details into profiles.

Start by searching for your name, phone number, email address and home address on major people-search sites. If you find a profile, look for the site's opt-out or removal process and submit a request to have your information deleted.

You can also use a data removal service to automate some of this work. These services send removal requests to data brokers on your behalf and may continue monitoring for information that reappears later.
Whichever route you choose, check back periodically. Personal information can resurface as data brokers refresh their databases or pull from new sources.
Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com.
Kurt's key takeaways

I doubt most HOA boards are thinking about scammers when they post meeting minutes or maintain a community directory. They are focused on running the neighborhood. The problem comes when information collected for one purpose becomes useful to someone with very different intentions. That is why I would spend a few minutes searching your HOA's name along with your own. See what a stranger can learn about you without logging in or proving they live in your community. You may be surprised by how quickly a name, home address and neighborhood can be connected. I would also ask your HOA what stays behind a resident login, what appears on the open web and what you can opt out of sharing. Laws vary by state, but there is no reason to make a scammer's research easier than it already is. And remember, removing something from an HOA website may only solve part of the problem. Once personal information spreads to people-search sites and data brokers, cutting down those profiles can help put some distance between you and anyone trying to build a convincing story around your life.

title: Floating solar panels could save cities millions. Is your town next?
summary: Lima, Ohio, has installed 3,120 floating solar panels on its Twin Lakes Reservoir, projecting nearly $10 million in electricity cost savings.
story: Fox News host Will Cain discusses Cowboy Space Corporation’s plans to launch solar-powered data centers into orbit by 2028 as demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure grows. Cain explains how the technology could use solar energy to power AI chips in space.

What if your town could build a solar farm without giving up acres of valuable land? Lima, Ohio, is trying something different. The city has completed a 2-megawatt solar array that floats on the Twin Lakes Reservoir, its primary drinking water source.

More than 3,000 solar panels now sit on the water and feed electricity to the nearby water treatment plant. The city projects the system will save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over its lifetime. That kind of savings could get the attention of cities far beyond Ohio.
So, could floating solar panels eventually show up on a reservoir near you? Here's how the technology works, why cities are interested and what it could mean for your community.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE
An Ohio city is using floating solar panels on its drinking water reservoir to power its water treatment plant and cut millions in projected energy costs. (D3Energy)
Ohio puts 3,120 solar panels on a drinking water reservoir

Lima officially celebrated the completion of its Twin Lakes Floating Solar Project on Aug. 12. The final system includes 3,120 solar panels spread across about 3.6 acres of water, according to developer D3Energy. The 2-megawatt array sits on Lima's primary drinking water reservoir. That reservoir serves roughly 35,000 residents.

Next door, the city's water treatment plant processes about 14 million gallons of water each day. It also consumes more electricity than any other city facility. That makes the plant an obvious place to look for energy savings. Lima projects the floating solar system will save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over its lifetime. Earlier city estimates put first-year savings at roughly $200,000. For a city utility, that is serious money. Actual lifetime savings will depend on factors including future electricity prices and how the system performs over time.
How floating solar panels work
Instead of attaching panels to racks planted in the ground, engineers mount them on floating platforms. Anchors and mooring lines keep the array in position.

Lima uses Ciel & Terre's Hydrelio floating system. Its anchoring setup connects to the banks and reservoir bottom. The design also allows the array to move as water levels change. The project uses bifacial solar panels, which can capture light on both sides.

Electricity travels from the array to eight inverters onshore. From there, the electricity helps power the water treatment plant. The result looks a bit like a traditional solar farm that traded grass for water.
Why cities may want solar panels floating on water

Here is where the idea gets particularly interesting. Land costs money. It also competes with housing, businesses, agriculture and other development. Reservoirs already occupy space. Lima's floating array covers about four acres.

A land-based system producing the same amount of electricity would reportedly need at least 10 acres. That could make floating solar attractive to cities with limited open space. The panels can also sit near the facilities that need the electricity. In Lima, the water treatment plant sits right beside the reservoir. That reduces the need to find a distant solar site and then figure out how to move the electricity where the city needs it.

Researchers have also studied whether floating solar can help reduce evaporation by shading portions of the water surface. Of course, every reservoir comes with different conditions. Water depth, changing levels and recreational use can affect whether a project makes sense. Federal researchers also consider existing dam operations when evaluating potential sites.
LAWMAKERS TARGET ENERGY AFFORDABILITY THROUGH SWEEPING PERMITTING OVERHAUL IN NEW HOUSE BILL
Floating solar could help cities generate clean energy without using valuable land, but questions remain about long-term costs and water safety. (D3Energy)
What about putting solar panels on drinking water?

This was one of my first questions. These panels are floating on the same reservoir that provides drinking water to about 35,000 people. Lima's system uses Ciel & Terre Hydrelio floats made from high-density polyethylene, or HDPE.

Ciel & Terre says its floating system complies with the BS 6920:2000 standard for nonmetallic materials that come into contact with water intended for human consumption. Still, communities considering floating solar have more to evaluate than whether the structure can float safely.

The National Renewable Energy Laboratory has examined environmental and regulatory questions surrounding floating solar. Its research notes that projects can affect water bodies differently depending on the location. That means a system that works well on one reservoir may require a different design somewhere else.
The project cost millions before it could save millions

There is another number worth paying attention to. The Lima project cost about $5.3 million. Federal support played a substantial role in making the numbers work. The city received a $2.4 million Department of Energy grant. Combined with almost $900,000 in federal direct-pay tax credits, that support helped offset roughly half of the project's cost.

Those incentives covered a significant share of the upfront expense. That context is important when another city looks at Lima's projected $10 million in savings. A town considering floating solar would need to look at construction costs, financing and expected electricity production. Available incentives could change the calculation as well.

Lima began considering the project years before crews put panels on the water. City Council approved moving forward with the project in 2023. Construction began in 2025 before the system came online this August.
Could floating solar panels spread across America?

Lima may look unusual today, but floating solar has substantial room to grow. Ohio already has more than one project. D3Energy and ARP Solar completed a 1.5-megawatt floating array for Del-Co Water in Delaware, Ohio, in 2024. A 6-megawatt system in Monroeville is expected to come online before the end of 2026.

The bigger opportunity stretches far beyond Ohio. National Renewable Energy Laboratory researchers studied federally owned or regulated reservoirs across the U.S. They estimated those reservoirs have technical potential for 861 to 1,042 gigawatts of floating solar capacity.
That figure represents technical potential rather than a prediction that thousands of reservoirs will soon disappear under solar panels. Plenty of locations would never make sense.

Still, the scale helps explain why energy developers and local governments are taking a closer look at water. CyberGuy has covered this idea before on a much larger scale. India's Omkareshwar project showed how enormous floating solar installations can become. We have also seen developers rethink the shape of solar installations on land. One Texas company is building vertical solar towers designed to produce more power from a smaller footprint.
AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING
Cities across the U.S. are exploring floating solar as a way to reduce utility costs while making use of existing reservoirs. (D3Energy)
Will floating solar panels lower your utility bill?

Here is the part I would keep an eye on. Lima expects to save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over the project's lifetime. But that does not mean residents will suddenly see a cheaper water bill. The city could use those savings in different ways. Lower energy costs could help cover other expenses, pay for infrastructure upgrades or ease pressure on future rate increases.

So, if a floating solar project comes to your town, there is one question worth asking: Will any of those savings eventually make their way back to you? That answer could determine how much this technology really helps the people paying the bills.
What this means to you

You probably do not spend much time thinking about how much electricity your local water plant consumes. Yet you ultimately help pay for that electricity through taxes, utility rates or both. Floating solar gives cities another way to attack that expense without buying a huge parcel of land.

It also raises questions you should ask before cheering on a project. How much will it cost? How much electricity will it realistically generate? What happens to the savings? You should also ask what testing and monitoring will protect the water supply. Those answers will tell you whether a floating solar project makes financial sense for your community.
Kurt's key takeaways

What I like about Lima's floating solar project is how practical the idea feels. The city already owns the reservoir, and its water treatment plant right next door uses a huge amount of electricity. So instead of finding another piece of land for solar panels, Lima put them on the water. Then there is the projected $10 million in savings. That certainly gets my attention. I want to see whether those savings hold up over time and, more importantly, whether residents eventually benefit from them. Lima also gives other cities something real to look at. We are seeing communities experiment with new ways to generate and store energy, from floating solar to massive battery projects. And who knows? The next solar project in your town may end up floating right on the water.

Would you be comfortable with thousands of solar panels floating on your town's drinking water reservoir if officials said the project could save millions, or would you need to see more long-term evidence first? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: NBC reporter, pilot among the victims identified in deadly Los Angeles helicopter crash
summary: Journalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw were identified as victims of the NBC4 helicopter crash in Los Angeles' Chatsworth neighborhood.
story: WARNING: Graphic footage—Investigators are working on the site of a helicopter crash in the Chatsworth neighborhood of Los Angeles, Cali.
Two victims of a deadly Tuesday night helicopter crash in Los Angeles have been identified as journalist Eliana Moreno and pilot George Marciniw, NBC4 Los Angeles confirmed.
Moreno and Marciniw were employees of Angel City Air, a helicopter charter company that operated NBC Los Angeles' NewsChopper4, NBC4 reported.

The pair were covering a deadly bus crash in downtown Los Angeles when the helicopter, which NBC4 confirmed belonged to the network, lost altitude and crashed, killing a third person on the ground who has yet to be identified.
ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE
Eliana Moreno seen in a news helicopter. (Facebook/Eliana Moreno)
Moreno had been a stalwart of both NBC4 and Telemundo 52's aerial coverage for years, going by the moniker "Eli in the Heli."
She had worked closely with Marciniw since 2023, with the pair sharing social media photos of them working and dining together through the years.
Marciniw was, according to NBC4, a Southern California native who graduated from Burbank High School in 1974.
Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw pose together in front of NewsChopper4. (Facebook/George Marciniw)

"We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives," NBC4 and Telemundo 52 said in a statement.
AMAZON CARGO PLANE OVERRUNS MIAMI AIRPORT RUNWAY AND STRIKES 'MULTIPLE' VEHICLES; 5 DEAD, 5 INJURED
The chopper crashed between two buildings in Los Angeles' Chatsworth neighborhood, producing a large fireball and injuring a fourth person.
At least three people were killed when a helicopter crashed not far from a deadly bus crash in Los Angeles. (KABC)
The injured person was transported to a local hospital in unknown condition, Los Angeles Fire Department Capt. Branden Silverman told reporters.

"Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family," California Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote in a statement on X.
"Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight," he added.
DATA SHOWS AMAZON JET’S KEY BRAKING SYSTEMS DID NOT DEPLOY DURING DEADLY MIAMI CRASH: NTSB
Eliana Moreno poses on a helipad with Los Angeles in the background. (Facebook/Eliana Moreno)
The National Transportation Safety Bureau (NTSB) and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said they will be sending investigators to the crash site on Wednesday to probe the crash's cause.

title: Attempted Trump assassin Thomas Crooks’ behavior revealed ‘red flags’ before attack: former FBI agent
summary: FBI documents reveal Thomas Crooks was "spiraling" before the Trump assassination attempt, with witnesses noting erratic behavior and odd habits.
story: Former FBI special agent Jonathan Gilliam tells Fox News Digital that newly released files show Thomas Crooks was "spiraling into almost a manic or delusional state," and argues the investigation into his motive "should not be closed."

A former FBI agent says newly released federal documents show Thomas Crooks, the man who attempted to assassinate President Donald Trump, was "spiraling into an almost manic state" before the rally shooting.

The federal documents turned over to the Senate, first reported by the New York Post, show that people close to Crooks, who killed one person and seriously injured two others, noticed odd behavior in the weeks before the attack.
Former FBI Special Agent Jonathan Gilliam told Fox News Digital that the documents turned over to the Senate contained several "red flags" about Crooks.

"These are definitely examples of somebody who is mentally not stable and also somebody who was spiraling into almost a manic or delusional state," Gilliam said. "When you combine somebody who is delusional, somebody who's hearing voices and is having almost a manic type of episode... with potential influence either by persons that they're around or things that they see online... it's very possible that that is the large part of this equation that we just have not seen."
TWO YEARS AFTER BUTLER, THREATS AGAINST TRUMP KEEP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT IN SHARP FOCUS

Thomas Matthew Crooks was a 20-year-old from Bethel Park, Pennsylvania, who attempted to assassinate former President Donald Trump during a 2024 campaign rally before being shot and killed by Secret Service agents. (Obtained by Fox News Digital)

While Crooks was "never into explosives," an unclassified memo from the FBI states that an individual confronted him about "a gallon jug of something that he said was used to clean the bed of his 3D printer."

The individual, who was redacted in the documents, didn't believe Crooks' explanation as his "ears would flame red when he lied." It's unknown when the individual confronted Crooks about the gallon jug.
That same unidentified individual said that Crooks began to "get more agitated" as he got older and "talked to himself a lot."

title: Charlie Kirk's family alleges UVU knew of rooftop security risk before his assassination: legal filing
summary: Charlie Kirk's family alleges Utah Valley University failed to secure rooftops and ignored warnings before the Turning Point USA founder's fatal shooting.
story: Fox News' Claudia Cowan provides details on the Kirk family's notice of claim against the state of Utah and Utah Valley University one year after his killing. 'Fox & Friends' co-hosts and Fox News contributor James Gagliano weigh in.

Charlie Kirk's family has filed a notice of claim — a precursor to a lawsuit — against Utah Valley University, the state and key individuals involved in campus leadership and security decisions, alleging that their failures led to the Turning Point USA founder's wrongful death.

"The risk of a rooftop shooter should have been especially top-of-mind given the attempted assassination of President Trump, Charlie Kirk’s close friend and political ally, by a rooftop shooter the previous year," reads the filing, signed by Kirk family attorneys Loren Washburn, Brett Parkinson and Clifford Parkinson and dated Sept. 9.

In one alleged exchange cited in the filing, Turning Point USA organizers told UVU Police Chief Jeffrey Long that UVU students had informed them of rooftop access to the Sorenson Center, a building "pretty close" to where Kirk would be speaking the day he was killed — and directly west of the Losee Center, which is where his alleged killer fired the shot from.
CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION: TIMELINE OF UTAH CAMPUS SHOOTING, TYLER ROBINSON CHARGED

Charlie Kirk speaks at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025 in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)
"If this is true, it would be nice to either have it controlled access or allow one of my guys to be there as well," someone at TPUSA wrote to the chief, according to the filing. "If possible."
"I got you covered," was Long's alleged reply.
JUDGE IN ACCUSED ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON'S CASE EXPLAINS WHY DEATH PENALTY REMAINS ON TABLE IN WRITTEN ORDER
Read the notice:

Kirk, a 31-year-old father of two, was shot and killed on Sept. 10, 2025 in the campus courtyard, and authorities say a lone gunman took a sniper's perch on the Losee Center rooftop on the far side of the clearing. Lawyers for the suspect, 23-year-old Tyler Robinson, pleaded not guilty on his behalf at an arraignment nearly a year later.

"His murder was entirely preventable and, in fact, would not have happened had the State of Utah and UVU followed through on their stated security promises, which included protecting the rooftops surrounding the quad where Charlie was speaking," said Brett Parkinson, counsel for the Kirk family. "Those failures not only robbed Charlie Kirk of his life, but also robbed his family of their husband, father, son, and brother, with impacts that will compound for the rest of their lives."

Charlie Kirk appears at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025 in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

The prospective plaintiffs in the filing are Kirk's widow, Erika Kirk, and their two juvenile children. It also acknowledges potential claims from his parents, Robert and Kathryn. The filing does not specify monetary damages. In addition to the wrongful death claim, it also raises a claim of "state-created danger" under the U.S. Constitution.
UVU said it is "aware of the notice of claim," and that it "addresses legal matters consistent with our established processes."
"Our focus remains on supporting our campus community," the university said in a statement.
REMEMBERING CHARLIE KIRK: TURNING POINT USA'S ANDREW KOLVET REFLECTS ON CONSERVATIVE GROUP'S CHALLENGING YEAR

Kirk, who built TPUSA into the country's largest conservative campus and youth-oriented activist organization in the country, also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024. He had become a personal friend of the president's as well as other prominent figures, including leading Utah politicians, the notice continues.
Ladder and rooftop ledge leading to the roof of the Losee Center at Utah Valley University — with no security gate in place. (Stepheny Price/Fox News Digital)
As a result, he had detractors, faced death threats, and publicly spoke about that before his assassination.

"You should not have to walk around with security for your entire family and for myself just because you support a politician or political candidate or certain values," he said at an event in May 2025.
"We get death threats," he continued. "People want to murder us."
ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

Political violence was on the rise as Kirk geared up for TPUSA's 2025 campus speaking events, titled, "The American Comeback Tour." The filing references the numerous attempts on Trump's life, the home invasion hammer attack on California Rep. Nancy Pelosi's husband, Paul, and the murders of former Minnesota House Speaker Melissa Hortman and her husband, Mark.

The scene after shots were fired at an appearance by Charlie Kirk at Utah Valley University on Sept. 10, 2025 in Orem, Utah. Kirk, founder of Turning Point USA, was speaking at his "American Comeback Tour" when he was shot in the neck and killed. (Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)

"Tragically, the UVU Parties failed to rise to the occasion," the filing alleges. "Through a series of stunning failures and reckless decisions, the UVU Parties created a foreseeable danger to Charlie."
SURVEILLANCE VIDEO TIMELINE TRACKS ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN ACROSS UVU CAMPUS BEFORE FATAL ROOFTOP SHOT

The allegations include a failure to perform a meaningful risk assessment or understand the significance of Kirk's visit to the UVU campus. Campus police allegedly did not have a written security plan or hold a security briefing in advance.

The second was "walking [Kirk] into a fishbowl" — surrounded on all sides by tall buildings or other elevated positions. "The UVU Parties could have declined to approve the Tour event in the outdoor quad location, or could have moved the venue indoors or to a more secure location, as it had done for controversial speakers in the past," according to the filing. The school also failed to dedicate additional resources for the outdoor venue despite the allegedly greater risk.
A view of the location where Charlie Kirk was shot one year ago. (Alec Thornock for Fox News Digital)
TYLER ROBINSON HEARING ENDS WITHOUT RULING AS EVIDENCE DISMANTLES CHARLIE KIRK CONSPIRACY CLAIMS
There were only six campus police officers assigned to the event, while Kirk's appearance attracted roughly 3,000 spectators, according to the filing.

"On information and belief, [UVU Campus Police] Chief Jeffrey Long requested approval from then-UVU President, Astrid Tuminez, to allocate more than the six officers — which represented only 25% of the UVU police force — but his request was denied," the filing continues.
FRIEND OF CHARLIE KIRK LABELS COURTROOM EVIDENCE 'DEVASTATING' AFTER CHILLING SURVEILLANCE FOOTAGE SHOWN
New security measures have been added to the area where the alleged assassin shot and killed Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk. (Stepheny Price/Fox News Digital)
After the denial, campus police did not seek additional resources from neighboring departments, such as the Orem or Provo police departments, according to the filing.

"The UVU Parties’ planning was so deficient that when Mr. Kirk was shot first responders were not available and Mr. Kirk was transported to Timpanogos Regional Hospital in a private vehicle, not an ambulance," the notice continues.
CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSINATION: EXCLUSIVE PHOTOS SHOW PATH TO CAMPUS ROOFTOP WEEKS LATER AS ACCESS SCRUTINIZED

The school and its leaders also had "exclusive power" that TPUSA and Kirk's security team did not have, such as authority to create a security perimeter, use physical barriers, deploy metal detectors or use other "common sense safety measures like those utilized at sporting events on campus."
Area near the roof of the Losee Center on the campus of Utah Valley University. (Stepheny Price/Fox News Digital)
SEND US A TIP

Although the campus had a security camera system, footage was not monitored in real time, according to the filing — and there were no drones to monitor rooftops or any other part of the "sprawling outdoor event."

"After-the-fact review of the footage at the Preliminary Hearing in the criminal prosecution of the alleged shooter Tyler Robinson showed the shooter running across the roof of the Losee Building to a 'sniper’s nest,'" attorneys for the Kirk family wrote. "If such footage had been monitored in real-time, Kirk’s tragic death could have been avoided."

An approximation of the suspected movements of Tyler Robinson, Charlie Kirk's alleged assassin, based on court documents, video from the scene and conversations with law enforcement. (Google Maps, Fox News Digital)
LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Despite warnings to the police chief about rooftop access in the area, the Losee Center rooftop was not secured. This, according to the filing, happened despite the fact that students were known to frequent the rooftop and people often found discarded "beer bottles and other trash" or paraphernalia there.
Together, all the alleged failures placed Kirk's life in danger, according to the filing.

The pathway to the roof of the Losee Center at Utah Valley University remains largely unmonitored following the assassination of Turning Point USA founder Charlie Kirk. (Stepheny Price/Fox News Digital/Trent Nelson/The Salt Lake Tribune/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"He was legally entitled to believe that when the UVU Parties approved the Tour event to be held on campus on September 10, that the UVU Parties would only hold the event in a venue and with associated security measures that made the event safe for him to attend and participate in," the notice reads. "Instead, Mr. Kirk was exposed to the danger of a rooftop shooter that took his life."

title: US military releases footage of massive operation to rescue injured airman stranded inside Iran
summary: Newly released video from the U.S. military shows elite Air Force pararescue operators rescuing an injured F-15E Strike Eagle crewman stranded deep inside Iran earlier this year.
story: US military unveils dramatic footage of daring Dude 44 rescue deep inside Iran (Credit: U.S. Air Forces Central).

The U.S. military released dramatic new video on Tuesday showing parts of one of the largest combat search-and-rescue operations in its history, including the moment elite Air Force pararescue operators reached a badly injured American airman stranded deep inside Iran.

The footage documents portions of the massive April operation to rescue the two-man crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle, call sign Dude 44, after the fighter was shot down by an Iranian shoulder-fired missile.
The pilot, known as Dude44 Alpha, and the backseat weapons systems officer, Dude44 Bravo, ejected from the aircraft and landed miles apart, leaving both stranded inside Iran.

While Dude44 Alpha was rescued after a little more than six hours, Dude44 Bravo suffered a broken back, arm and shoulder after a damaged parachute led to a hard landing. He remained stranded for nearly two days before U.S. forces reached him.
HOLLYWOOD LEGEND MAKING MOVIE ABOUT EPIC IRAN RESCUE MISSION TO SAVE F-15 FIGHTER JET CREW

Newly released U.S. military video shows Air Force pararescue operators reaching Dude44 Bravo on a mountain ridgeline after the injured airman spent nearly two days stranded inside Iran. (U.S. Air Forces Central)
The newly released video shows U.S. military helicopters searching for Bravo as American forces worked to locate and recover him.
Despite his injuries, Bravo moved away from his landing site and began climbing toward a roughly 7,000-foot ridgeline as daylight revealed the desert valley and steep cliffs surrounding him.
The footage also shows American bombers and drones striking Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces that were in proximity to Bravo.
TRUMP RETALIATES AFTER IRAN ATTACK AS EXPERT WARNS REGIME IS GROWING MORE DANGEROUS
U.S. military helicopters search for Dude44 Bravo during a massive combat search-and-rescue operation after his F-15E Strike Eagle was shot down over Iran in April. (U.S. Air Forces Central)
"There was clear intent out of the Iranian ground force to come find those two guys," Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Dan Caine told CBS News this week.
The video then shows the dramatic moment on April 5 when two elite Air Force pararescue operators, known as PJs, reached the injured Bravo on the mountain ridgeline.
Two large search-and-rescue aircraft had landed on a makeshift desert runway before smaller "Little Bird" helicopters flew toward Bravo's position on the ridgeline.
Bravo called the moment he saw his rescuers "one of the greatest moments of my life."
HOW IRAN ATTACKS ARE FORCING THE PENTAGON TO RETHINK ITS DECADES-OLD MIDDLE EAST BASE STRATEGY

Newly released military footage shows U.S. bombers and drones striking Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces near Dude44 Bravo as American forces worked to rescue the stranded airman. (U.S. Air Forces Central)
"Let's go," he recalled telling them.
The second rescue operation put 92 U.S. service members on the ground in Iran, marking the first time American forces had boots on the ground in the country since 1980.

Hundreds of U.S. service members also supported the operation from the air, while between 3,000 and 5,000 service members supported the rescue mission overall, according to U.S. Central Command Commander Adm. Brad Cooper.
But the operation was not over once Bravo was reached.

The landing gear of the two rescue aircraft became trapped in the desert sand, stranding Bravo and more than 90 U.S. service members inside Iran. A clandestine Air Force unit was ultimately brought in to extract the group, CBS News reported.
Bravo was finally brought to safety roughly 50 hours after Dude 44 was shot down. The rescue was completed as the sun rose on Easter Sunday.

Two elite Air Force pararescue operators, known as PJs, reached the badly injured Dude44 Bravo on a roughly 7,000-foot ridgeline inside Iran. (U.S. Air Forces Central)
Fox News' Liz Friden and Fox News Digital's Stepheny Price contributed to this report.

title: Multiple death sentences in different states are set to be carried out within 24 hours: 'Not very common'
summary: Multiple U.S. executions in the U.S. are set within 24 hours this week, part of a surge that has seen 25 death penalty cases in 2026 with more to come.
story: Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher said it is rare for multiple executions to be carried out in numerous states within a couple days.
Multiple executions are scheduled in the U.S. in as many states within a 24-hour window this week.

Georgia and Texas had each planned to put a man to death within an hour of each other on Wednesday before a court stepped in to halt the one in Georgia for now, while Alabama is set to carry out another execution the following day. Texas remains scheduled to execute LeJames Norman on Wednesday after a Georgia judge stayed Stacey Humphreys' execution late Tuesday.

In the Peach State, 53-year-old Humphreys was set to be executed on Wednesday for his conviction in the 2003 murders of two real estate agents, 21-year-old Lori Brown and 33-year-old Cindy Williams. But a Cobb County judge stayed his execution late Tuesday, meaning the execution cannot move forward unless the stay is lifted or overturned by a higher court.
About an hour after that execution was initially set to happen, Texas scheduled to execute Norman, 40, for the triple murder of his neighbors during a robbery that turned deadly in 2005.
GEORGIA KILLER WHO MURDERED TWO SUBURBAN REAL ESTATE AGENTS FACES EXECUTION AFTER 23-YEAR WAIT FOR JUSTICE

Jeffery Lee, LeJames Norman and Stacey Humphreys have execution dates scheduled, although Humphreys' execution has been stayed by a Georgia judge, in three different states within a 24-hour window. (Alabama Department of Corrections:Texas Department of Criminal Justice:Georgia Department of Corrections)
Then on Thursday, Alabama plans to execute Jeffery Lee, 50, for a double murder carried out during a 1998 pawn shop holdup.

"It's not very common to have this many executions just across a couple of days," Death Penalty Information Center Executive Director Robin Maher told Fox News Digital. "This month, the month of September, we have seven executions scheduled. Last year, in October, we had seven executions in a single month. But before then, we'd have to go back all the way to 2010 to see that number in a single month."

"Just earlier this year, in August, there were three executions on the same day," she continued. "This is an unusual year in that we're seeing occurrences like a number of executions scheduled on the same day or during the same month. But there's no evidence there's any coordination among the states to have all these executions occur simultaneously. This looks largely to be a coincidence."

On Aug. 13, three states — Tennessee, Oklahoma and Alabama — carried out three lethal injections on the same day, marking the first time three states executed prisoners on the same day since January 7, 2010.
Weeks earlier, on July 28, Florida carried out two executions in a single day, which was the Sunshine State's first double execution in decades.
FLORIDA EXECUTES 74-YEAR-OLD FOR WIFE'S MURDER, BECOMING OLDEST INMATE PUT TO DEATH IN STATE'S MODERN HISTORY

Texas is scheduled to execute LeJames Norman on Wednesday after a Georgia judge stayed Stacey Humphreys' execution, while Alabama is set to carry out another execution the following day. (AP Photo/Sue Ogrocki)

In 2026, 25 executions have been carried out in the U.S., and 14 are scheduled for the remainder of the year, although that number could change if courts issue stays or states schedule additional executions.
Last year, 11 states carried out 47 executions, making up the most executions carried out in a single year in the U.S. since 2009.

Leading the way in executions is Florida, which set a record with 19 inmates put to death in 2025, more than 40% of the U.S. total for the year. It also carried out 15 so far in 2026, accounting for 60% of this year's total across the country.
Across 2025 and 2026 thus far, Florida accounts for about 47% of the nation’s executions, as it continues its accelerated pace amid a flurry of death warrants signed by Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis.

Texas, Alabama and South Carolina followed Florida, with eight, six and five executions, respectively, in that window. Texas carried out five executions in 2025 and three so far in 2026, Alabama executed five people in 2025 and one in 2026 and South Carolina put five people to death — all in 2025.
In 2026, 25 executions have been carried out in the U.S., and 14 are scheduled for the remainder of the year. (The Promise of Justice Initiative via AP)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Last year was a very unusual year. It was the most executions we've seen in 15 years in the United States," Maher said. "This year, we do not expect to reach that number of executions again. There are a number of other warrants that are still open for this year, but I don't think we'll reach the high that we reached last year."

"All of this is really due to Florida," she added. "Gov. DeSantis has decided that he wants to set a record in the number of executions that are conducted during his term. He has scheduled an execution for roughly every two weeks in the state of Florida, both last year and this year."

Two executions remain scheduled in Florida for the rest of 2026. Curtis Beasley, 77, is set to be executed Sept. 29 for the 1995 murder of a woman who was bludgeoned with a hammer, while William Lee Thompson, 74, is scheduled for execution Oct. 13 for the 1976 murder of a woman who was beaten, tortured and killed with a chain-link belt.

title: 3 dead, 1 hospitalized after news helicopter crashes in Los Angeles commercial area
summary: Three people are dead, and one person is hospitalized after a news helicopter crashed between two commercial buildings in the Chatsworth area of Los Angeles, authorities said.
story: WARNING: Graphic footage—Investigators are working on the site of a helicopter crash in the Chatsworth neighborhood of Los Angeles, Cali.
Three people are dead, and one person is hospitalized after a news helicopter crashed Tuesday night in Los Angeles, authorities said.
The Los Angeles Fire Department said more than 70 firefighters responded just before 7 p.m. to the crash between two commercial buildings at 9151 N. Mason Ave. in Chatsworth.

NBC Los Angeles confirmed that the helicopter involved was its NewsChopper4. The aircraft was providing aerial coverage of a deadly crash involving a bus and an SUV in the Chatsworth area of Los Angeles when it went down.
PENNSYLVANIA STATE POLICE HELICOPTER, SMALL PLANE COLLIDE IN MIDAIR, KILLING 1 AND INJURING 2 STATE TROOPERS
At least three people were killed when a helicopter crashed not far from a deadly bus crash in Los Angeles. (KABC)
Three people were pronounced dead at the scene of the helicopter crash and a fourth was transported to a local hospital in unknown condition, according to the department.

One of the victims was a pedestrian in the parking lot, according to LAFD Capt. Branden Silverman. The other two victims were aboard the helicopter and have since been identified as Angel City Air employees Eliana Moreno and George Marciniw, according to NBC4.

Moreno was an aerial photojournalist for NBC4 and its Spanish-language sister station, Telemundo 52. She joined Angel City Air’s helicopter team in 2010 after graduating from Chapman University with a degree in broadcast journalism and political science, according to the station.
Marciniw, the helicopter's pilot, grew up in Southern California and graduated from Burbank High School, according to NBC4.
First responders work the scene after a helicopter crashed near a bus crash in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in Los Angeles, Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Ethan Swope)
The crash sparked a fire that damaged four vehicles and two storage containers before firefighters extinguished the flames, according to LAFD. No nearby structures were exposed to the fire.

The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration said they will be investigating the cause of the helicopter crash and would be sending one of its investigators on Wednesday.
GOP GOV CANDIDATE RECOUNTS MIRACLE WATER LANDING AS DISPATCH AUDIO REVEALS DESPERATE SEARCH FOR SINKING PLANE
First responders work the scene after a helicopter crashed near a bus crash in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in Los Angeles, Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Ethan Swope)
Local outlets reported that several TV news helicopters were in the area covering a Metro bus crash that left at least two people dead and multiple others hospitalized.
Colleen Williams, an anchor for NBC4, confirmed on air that the station's NewsChopper4 had crashed.
"We are going to take a couple of minutes to think about that, process it," Williams said, before the station's coverage cut away.
AMAZON CARGO JET PILOT REPORTEDLY TOLD WIFE, 'MY CAREER IS OVER' SHORTLY AFTER DEADLY CRASH
NBC4 and Telemundo 52 issued a joint statement following the deadly helicopter crash.

"We are deeply saddened to share that a helicopter providing aerial news coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52 was involved in a fatal accident in Los Angeles on Tuesday evening. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the families, friends and colleagues of those who lost their lives."

Emergency crews respond to a deadly Metro bus crash in Chatsworth, Los Angeles, that local outlets said several TV news helicopters had been covering before NBC4's NewsChopper4 crashed nearby. (Getty Images)
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass mourned the victims of both crashes.

"I’m absolutely devastated by the loss of life in Chatsworth tonight," Bass said in a statement. "My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we lost in the tragic bus collision and helicopter crash."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Multiple people were killed when a helicopter crashed not far from a deadly bus crash in Los Angeles. (KABC)
California Gov. Gavin Newsom also responded to the deadly crashes.

"Our hearts are with the victims and families of tonight’s devastating Metro bus and helicopter crashes in Chatsworth, and with the entire NBC4 family," Newsom said. "Thank you to the first responders working tirelessly tonight."

title: Fourth Florida resident dies after contracting flesh-eating bacteria linked to oysters
summary: Florida reports fourth Vibrio vulnificus death in 2026 as health officials warn about raw oysters, contaminated water and severe infections.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel warns beachgoers about the rise of Vibrio vulnificus, a deadly flesh-eating bacterium found in warm salt waters.
A fourth person in Florida has died after contracting flesh-eating bacteria commonly linked to consuming raw or undercooked oysters, health officials said.
The death was included Thursday in the Florida Department of Health's updated fatality count for the deadly flesh-eating bacterium Vibrio vulnificus.
The individual was from Broward County and between the ages of 75 and 79, WSFA reported. It remains unclear exactly how the person contracted the infection.
Previous deaths were attributed to residents of Bay, Palm Beach and Marion counties, according to the state’s health department.
BEACHGOERS WARNED AFTER DEADLY 'FLESH-EATING' BACTERIA KILLS 5 IN SOUTHERN STATE
Florida health officials warned that eating raw or undercooked oysters can lead to infection with Vibrio vulnificus, a flesh-eating bacterium. (iStock)
"Most people get vibriosis by eating raw or undercooked shellfish, particularly oysters," the Florida Department of Health said.
According to the department's website, Florida has reported 21 cases of Vibrio vulnificus in 2026.
In the last 10 years, 2022 and 2024 reported some of the highest numbers of cases and deaths in the region. Florida recorded 19 deaths and 82 cases in 2024, while 2022 saw 17 deaths and 74 cases.
NORTH CAROLINA MOUNTAIN COMMUNITY BRACES FOR HURRICANE SEASON TWO YEARS AFTER HELENE'S BRUTAL IMPACT

Officials said the unusual increase stemmed from certain counties experiencing impacts from hurricanes Helene and Ian. Severe weather events that cause standing or floodwaters pose a risk of exposure to the bacteria, officials said.
Vibrio vulnificus is a naturally occurring bacterium found in warm, brackish seawater.
POPULAR BEACHES CLOSED AS HIGH BACTERIA LEVELS RAISE HEALTH CONCERNS FOR SWIMMERS
Vibrio vulnificus bloodstream infections are fatal about 50% of the time, according to Florida health officials. (CDC.gov)
Exposure can occur when a person eats oysters contaminated with the bacteria or enters contaminated water with an open wound.
Health officials said bloodstream infections caused by Vibrio vulnificus are fatal about 50% of the time.
While healthy individuals typically develop a mild illness, Vibrio vulnificus infections can cause severe illness in people with weakened immune systems.

"A recent study showed that people with these pre-existing medical conditions were 80 times more likely to develop Vibrio vulnificus bloodstream infections than healthy people," Florida health officials said.
'I THOUGHT I HAD THE FLU': MOM NEARLY DIED AFTER DISMISSING DEADLY SEPSIS SYMPTOMS

In this aerial view, a person walks through floodwaters that inundated a neighborhood after Hurricane Milton came ashore on Oct. 10, 2024, in Punta Gorda, Florida. Flooding and standing water can increase the risk of exposure to Vibrio vulnificus, health officials said. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Severe infections can cause symptoms including fever, chills, decreased blood pressure, also known as septic shock, and blistering skin lesions. In some cases, wound infections can lead to tissue damage requiring amputation.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Elsewhere along the Gulf Coast, Louisiana has reported 15 cases and six deaths this year as of Sept. 9, according to the Louisiana Department of Health. Fourteen of the cases were attributed to wound or seawater exposure.
The Texas Department of State Health Services says Texas typically sees an average of 33 cases per year.
Mississippi reported three cases as of August, according to the state’s health department.
Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Injured climber crawls ‘through the night’ to safety after falling 500 feet down California mountain
summary: Mount Shasta rescue crews finds San Jose man in a remote cabin after a glissading accident at Shasta-Trinity National Forest.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

A California climber who suffered significant injuries after falling 500 feet down Mount Shasta spent the night crawling to a remote cabin, where he was found by rescue crews the following day, forest officials said Friday.

The San Jose man, who was not identified, lost control while sliding down Avalanche Gulch, a steep, snow and ice-covered route, Thursday night after reaching the summit in the Shasta-Trinity National Forest.

"The climber told rescuers that he had attempted to glissade down the mountain, lost control, and slid approximately 500 feet. During his fall, he sustained several significant lacerations and injuries to his feet," forest service officials said.
Authorities added that the climber was unable to call for help because his cellphone died shortly after summiting.
MOUNTAIN CLIMBER SURVIVES TERRIFYING 500-FOOT FALL IN CALIFORNIA'S SIERRA NEVADA, NIGHT STRANDED ON LEDGE
The climber lost control while glissading down Avalanche Gulch and crawled through the night after removing his boots. (U.S. Forest Service / Shasta-Trinity National Forest)
Due to the painful swelling that occurred after the fall, the climber reportedly removed his boots and "crawled through the night" down the remainder of Avalanche Gulch to Horse Camp Cabin.
By the next day, his friends were unable to contact him and reported him missing to the Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Office.
Rescue teams and air support were mobilized across several agencies by 2 p.m. Friday, and began searching the Avalanche Gulch area, officials said.
Two hours later, they were alerted that the climber was inside Horse Camp Cabin after a hiker entered the cabin and found him there.
MISSOURI DEPUTY AG, MISSING 6 DAYS AFTER SEEKING TO SUMMIT WYOMING'S TALLEST PEAK, IS FOUND ALIVE
Officials praised the climber for knowing the route, notifying friends of his plans and making his way to Horse Camp Cabin. (U.S. Forest Service / Shasta-Trinity National Forest)
Officials used the incident to remind hikers to allow plenty of daylight for their hikes, establish a turnaround time around noon, carry backup electronics and be prepared to self-rescue.

"The climber did his best to self-rescue despite significant injuries, and knew his route well enough without a map, to find his way back to the Horse Camp Cabin. Never rely solely on a GPS or phone to navigate – if those devices stop working, your own navigation skills will be critical in ensuring a safe return home," officials said.
They further commended the climber for notifying his friends of his whereabouts before he went missing.

"The climber wisely notified his friends of his plan to climb Mount Shasta and made a point to check in and provide progress updates. When he lost contact, his friends contacted law enforcement to report him overdue and traveled to help with the search effort. It is always advisable to notify at least one person of your itinerary," officials said.
CLIMBER STRANDED ON 6-INCH LEDGE AT 11,000 FEET AS 46 MPH WINDS GROUND RESCUE HELICOPTER
Friends contacted authorities after the climber failed to check in, prompting a multi-agency search near Mount Shasta. (U.S. Forest Service — Shasta-Trinity National Forest)
The rescue team was assisted by the Mount Shasta Climbing Rangers, Siskiyou County Sheriff’s Search and Rescue, and a California Highway Patrol helicopter crew.
The incident marks the latest rescue operation in the Northern California forest, where rescue teams respond to numerous incidents annually.
According to the mountain’s website, the route to the summit via Avalanche Gulch is steep and rigorous, requiring proper equipment and snow-travel skills.

title: Arizona man says he lost $475k home to HOA foreclosure over less than $1,000 in unpaid dues
summary: Toby Newton says his Mesa HOA refused payment arrangements on just $977 in unpaid dues, then sold his $475,000 home at auction for only $8,172.
story: Toby Newton says his home was foreclosed on after falling behind on HOA dues and that his attempts to arrange a payment plan were rejected.
An Arizona man had his $475,000 home sold from under him by his homeowners' association (HOA) after falling behind on his dues, which amounted to less than $1,000.

Toby Newton, 53, purchased the four-bedroom home in Mesa in 2022, but fell behind on his quarterly HOA dues after losing his sales job and being diagnosed with diabetes, he told Fox News Digital. In addition, his partner has been battling breast cancer, he said.

"I was a year and a half behind because of the situation I found myself in with my girlfriend and myself getting sick," Newton said. "That's how it started. I called the HOA to make an arrangement with them to get them paid and they wouldn't talk to me. They told me I had to talk to their attorney and that's when it blew up."
83-YEAR-OLD WINS SETTLEMENT AFTER HONOLULU SLAPPED HER WITH $590K FINE OVER WEBSITE GLITCH
Toby Newton's Mesa, Arizona home was sold after his HOA began foreclosure proceedings because he owned less than $1,000 in dues, he said. (Toby Newton)
Newton paid about $170 to the HOA every three months, eventually owing $977 after getting into financial trouble.
Fox News Digital has reached out to the HOA's attorney.

Newton reportedly contacted the Superstition Springs Community Master Association in an effort to work out a payment so he could catch up on his dues. Initially, he offered to pay an extra $50 per month on top of his monthly assessments in an effort to chip away at his debt.
That was denied, he said.
83-YEAR-OLD WOMAN SUES HONOLULU AFTER WEBSITE ERROR TURNED INTO $590K NIGHTMARE
A monthly increase of $200 was also rebuffed, he said. The HOA eventually began foreclosure proceedings.
"I just don't understand how an HOA that's supposed to be there for the community doesn't work with the community at all," Newton said.

Meanwhile, the debt ballooned to nearly $10,000, Newton said, mostly for attorney's fees for the HOA. The home was sold at a public auction in November 2025 for just $8,172, the Mesa Tribune reported.

"The sale happened and I'm still in the house," said Newton. "I haven't been kicked out yet. That's what I'm trying to avoid. I'm just trying to save it because I don't know how it could go from owing them $977 to $10,000."

Toby Newton sits inside the living of his Mesa, Arizona home. His homeowners association took action against him after he fell behind his quarterly dues by less than $1,000, Newton said. (Toby Newton)
Newton said he wasn't aware of the auction until two days before. He said he has no plans to leave the home, which he purchased to spend his golden years after retirement.
"We are holding on to hope that we may still have a chance to buy our home back," an online fundraiser created by Newton and his partner states.
TRUMP SCORES MAJOR WIN AS CONGRESS PASSES HOUSING CRACKDOWN ON WALL STREET INVESTORS
HOAs have long been accused of abusing their authority and fining, or even foreclosing on homeowners, for committing even the most mundane violations.

Across the country, many HOAs are taking a tougher stance on unpaid dues amid mounting financial pressures. Real estate experts have said the aggressive collection efforts are being driven by rising operating costs, shrinking reserve funds, and concerns that unpaid assessments could leave associations unable to cover essential expenses, FOX Business previously reported.

HOA-related foreclosures have jumped nearly 40% compared with two years earlier, The Wall Street Journal reported in August.

title: Former Ohio teacher charged after missing teen found at his home 263 days later: reports
summary: Authorities allege Jobe Binkley knowingly allowed a missing teenage girl to stay at his home for months despite knowing she had been reported missing.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A former Ohio teacher has been charged after authorities alleged he knowingly allowed a missing underage teen girl to stay at his home despite being aware she had been reported missing.

Jobe Binkley, 48, of Springfield, Ohio, has been charged with one count of interference with custody, a first-degree misdemeanor punishable by up to six months in jail and a $1,000 fine, according to a criminal complaint obtained by Fox News Digital.
The girl had been missing for 263 days after running away from a youth shelter in Columbus on Dec. 2, 2025, WSYX and The New York Post reported.
The outlets reported Binkley was the girl's former high school science teacher.
CALIFORNIA FOOTBALL COACH ARRESTED AFTER STUDENTS MAKE DISTURBING DISCOVERY AT SCHOOL
According to the complaint, officers alleged Binkley "did knowingly allow the child victim to stay in his home while having knowledge of the victim being an active missing juvenile." (Getty Images)
According to the complaint, Binkley "did knowingly allow the child victim to stay in his home while having knowledge of the victim being an active missing juvenile."

A probable cause affidavit states that on Aug. 21, an officer working as an agent of the U. S. Marshal's Office went to Binkley's Springfield home after investigators identified it as the girl's last known location.
According to the affidavit, Binkley told the officer the teen was inside the residence and called for her to come outside, which she did.
"He spoke with the resident owner, Jobe Binkley, who stated the juvenile was inside. He called for the juvenile, and they exited the home," the affidavit states.
BROOKLYN TEACHERS WHO WITNESSED 9/11 AS CHILDREN REVEAL WHAT THEY WANT THE NEXT GENERATION TO REMEMBER
Investigators also alleged officers had gone to Binkley's home on two earlier occasions while searching for the missing girl. (Clark County Jail)
Investigators also alleged officers had gone to Binkley's home on two earlier occasions while searching for the missing girl.
During those visits, Binkley allegedly refused to let officers inside and told them the juvenile was not there.
"Officers had been to Mr. Binkley's house on two previous occasions where the juvenile was entered missing," the affidavit states.
"At those times he refused officers to enter his home and stated that the missing person was not inside. Officers noted that Jobe was made aware the individual was in fact an active missing person."
According to The New York Post, Binkley was placed on administrative leave from Springfield City Schools in November 2024 and again in January 2025 before he was fired the following month.
FORMER TEXAS HIGH SCHOOL TEACHER ARRESTED AFTER PROBE INTO INAPPROPRIATE STUDENT RELATIONSHIP
The Clark County Municipal Court in Springfield, Ohio, where Jobe Binkley is expected to appear for a pretrial hearing Sept. 30. (Google Maps)
Chelsi Warner, the mother of the victim's half-sister, alleged to the New York Post that Binkley began grooming the teen after they met at school.
"She’s had a troubled history with her mother and this groomer took advantage of a girl looking for a parental figure," Warner said.
Court records show Binkley has pleaded not guilty to the charge.  A pretrial hearing has been scheduled for Sept. 30, according to court records.

The Springfield Police Department and Springfield City Schools could not immediately be reached by Fox News Digital for comment.
